Briar.name: Briar
questions: What grows by the river?
What are you trying to grow?
Briar.local: Mint. It survives my experiments, which is a very high standard.
personal: I keep notes on every seed I plant.
I want a flower that can survive the wind off the Coast.
My first coastal seedlings all died. I kept their labels anyway. They taught me more than the ones that grew.

Mira.name: Mira
questions: Where do people meet?
What do you listen for?
Mira.local: Wayfarer’s Rest. A pot of tea will get a conversation started before I can.
personal: I like hearing what people notice first about town.
Sailors tell stories starting with the weather. Miners start with whoever forgot the lantern.
I write down ordinary days, too. If all we remember are disasters and triumphs, we forget what we came home for.

Alden.name: Alden
questions: What’s beyond the east bridge?
Do you like exploring?
Alden.local: The Wayfarer trail. I stay near the bridge when the woods get quiet.
personal: I like deciding where to turn back.
I used to follow the river because a path that runs both ways feels safer.
I take a different turn each week now. I still mark the way home.

Pip.name: Pip
questions: What do you play at the pavilion?
Where do you get your ideas?
Pip.local: Board games. My best move is asking for a rematch before I lose.
personal: I sketch little puzzles on scrap paper.
I made a game about crossing Oldwater Lake without waking the fish.
I left a way for both players to win. It took three weeks before anyone tried it.

Clover.name: Clover
questions: What’s worth seeing at the market?
Do you collect anything?
Clover.local: Look at what the stallholders put out first. It’s usually what they’re proudest of.
personal: Buttons. You’d be surprised how many good ones go unclaimed.
The blue ones remind me of Folded Coast.
I’m sewing them onto a coat for myself. For once I’m making something I get to keep.

Flint.name: Flint
questions: What should I bring to Deepwell?
What do you like fixing?
Flint.local: Light, and enough patience to stop when you can’t see what you’re doing.
personal: Anything with a screw I can actually reach.
My first cart repair squeaked louder than the broken wheel.
I kept the wheel. It reminds me that a good repair should make someone’s day quieter.

Hazel.name: Hazel
questions: What do you do when rain won’t stop?
Why gardening?
Hazel.local: Check the beds and leave the seedlings alone. They don’t need an audience.
personal: I like work with a clear beginning.
I was terrible at waiting until I started keeping a garden.
The healthiest bed is the one I check least often. I’m still learning from that.

Theo.name: Theo
questions: Where do stories come from?
Which stories are yours?
Theo.local: Half come off a boat. The other half start with someone saying they have nothing to tell.
personal: The short ones are usually true.
I once took the wrong trail out of the Grove and ended up back at my own lunch spot.
I used to leave that part out. These days it’s my favourite part.

Nell.name: Nell
questions: Any advice for Oldwater Lake?
Why fish so early?
Nell.local: Watch the water between casts. It’ll tell you when the fish are moving.
personal: No one asks me to hurry before dawn.
I started going before sunrise because I was afraid of missing the best bite.
Now I’d go even if I forgot the rod. That hour belongs to me.

Rowe.name: Rowe
questions: Is the town always this busy?
Where do you go for quiet?
Rowe.local: No. Sometimes everyone is indoors arguing about whose turn it is to make tea.
personal: I take the pond path and count the lamps.
I used to go farther, out toward the Wayfarer bridge.
The pond’s close enough that people know where to find me. I’m glad they do.

Fern.name: Fern
questions: What do you read about?
Do you travel, too?
Fern.local: The realms. I’m making a list of things two travellers saw differently.
personal: A little. A good book never gave me wet boots.
The first time I saw Silverfall, I’d read so much that I forgot to look up.
I closed the book and stayed until the light changed. That never made it into anyone’s guide.

Kit.name: Kit
questions: What’s the quickest way across town?
What do you like delivering?
Kit.local: Learn where people stop to talk. The straight line is rarely the fast one.
personal: The little parcels. They’re less work and usually more important.
I once carried a repaired lantern to the Coast and brought a shell back.
I keep the shell on my desk so I remember a trip can go both ways.

Wren.name: Wren
questions: When can I hear music?
What do you play?
Wren.local: Wednesday evening in the square. You can listen from the edge if you like.
personal: Anything I can remember without looking at my hands.
I stole a rhythm from the watermill. The wheel didn’t mind.
I play it slower now. It sounds like the river when there’s nobody around.

Bram.name: Bram
questions: What’s it like at the western cliffs?
Do you go underground?
Bram.local: Listen before you speak. The cave will answer either way.
personal: Only when someone is expecting me back.
I once missed the last lamp and had to follow my own footsteps out.
I check the lamps on my walk now. Nobody asked me to. I just like knowing they’re lit.

Lark.name: Lark
questions: What do you see around the pond?
What would you like to see?
Lark.local: Mostly ripples. Everything worth seeing waits until I lower the notebook.
personal: The shorebirds along Folded Coast.
I drew one from a description once. It looked like a spoon with opinions.
I finally saw one. Mine was wrong about everything except the attitude.

Juniper.name: Juniper
questions: What’s good at the Food Stand?
What do you cook?
Juniper.local: Ask Moss what’s still warm. That’s always the right order.
personal: Food that forgives being left on the stove.
I tried making a Coast stew from memory and forgot the salt.
It was the first meal I shared with my neighbours. Nobody mentioned the salt until the next week.

Tess.name: Tess
questions: What are you drawing today?
What do you keep in your notebook?
Tess.local: The Starlace Tree. The shape is different depending on where I stand.
personal: Mostly things that won’t sit still.
I tried drawing the portal light. Every time I looked down it had changed.
I kept the worst sketch. It was the first one that felt like watching it.

Oak.name: Oak
questions: Where’s the best view?
Do you ever get nervous up there?
Oak.local: The lookout. You can follow the river until the rooftops get in the way.
personal: Only on the way down.
I used to climb for the view. Now I climb to check the weather.
Once I waited up there for a friend’s boat. I waved long before they could see me.

Ada.name: Ada
questions: Can I join the next game?
Do you like winning?
Ada.local: Yes. If someone says the rules are obvious, ask them to explain the first turn.
personal: I like a good last turn.
My favourite games leave you with something to talk about afterward.
I keep a spare seat open. Someone who thought they were just watching might change their mind.

Finch.name: Finch
questions: What’s on the town map?
Do you make maps?
Finch.local: Landmarks and paths. Look for the board by the Starlace Tree.
personal: I copy routes so I can mark where I got confused.
My first map of the Coast had a rock that turned out to be a boat.
I still draw it in the margin. It reminds me to ask what moves.

Ash.name: Ash
questions: Which trail do you like?
What do you do out there?
Ash.local: The one across the east bridge, just far enough for town to go quiet.
personal: I stop walking for a while.
The Grove used to make me uneasy. I thought quiet meant I was alone.
Now I can hear how much is going on when I stand still.

elder.name: Elder Ram
questions: What holds Crossroads together?
What was town like when you arrived?
elder.local: The portal brings people through. The neighbours give them a reason to come back.
personal: The paths were narrower. We still argued about where to put the benches.
I used to know the realms better than the people who lived next door.
I stopped keeping a count of places I’d been. I started keeping a list of people I wanted to see again.

bartle.name: Bartle
questions: What should I pack?
How did you get into supplies?
bartle.local: Buy for the problem you keep running into. It’s cheaper than packing for every possible disaster.
personal: I got very good at forgetting one important thing.
I reached Deepwell once with three spare buckles and no lamp oil.
Now I lay out the basics first. If you leave my shop with fewer things and a better plan, I did my job.

Moss.name: Moss
questions: What’s good before a trip?
How did you learn to cook?
Moss.local: Something you’ll actually remember to eat. I can help with the first part.
personal: I started by making soup for people on late shifts.
A boat crew from Oldwater once taught me to season fish without drowning it in salt.
I still cook a little extra on cold evenings. Someone will come back hungrier than they expected.

Tessa.name: Tessa
questions: What helps after a hard run?
What’s the hardest part of the work?
Tessa.local: Sit down first. Then tell me what hurts. In that order.
personal: Convincing people that resting counts as doing something.
When I first worked near the Grove, I thought I had to fix everything before sunset.
I learned to tell people when I didn’t know. It helped them trust me when I did.

Scout_Alden.name: Scout Alden
questions: How should I choose a realm?
What’s your favourite route?
Scout_Alden.local: Pick the trip you can get home from. The hardest route can wait.
personal: I like the first stretch of the Wayfarer trail.
I once turned back at Silverfall because I’d lost the light. I was embarrassed for a week.
The next time, I took someone who’d never seen it. I’m glad I saved that view.

Rowan.name: Rowan
questions: What makes a good seed?
What’s your favourite crop?
Rowan.local: One you’re willing to check even after you’ve forgotten what you planted.
personal: I like pears. They make a good excuse to come back.
I used to swap seeds at the lake and forget to write down who gave me what.
There’s a bed I call the borrowed garden. I can tell you where every seed came from now.

Brin.name: Brin
questions: What’s good bait today?
Do you fish on your days off?
Brin.local: Have a look at the tray. I’m always trying something different when the river changes.
personal: Of course. I just don’t count the catch.
I started trading after a stranger shared their last hook with me.
I keep a spare in my apron. It’s amazing how often the next person needs one.

Lio.name: Lio
questions: What’s the harbour like at night?
Do you like the late shift?
Lio.local: Quiet enough to hear a boat before you can see it. Bring a light.
personal: I like having time to finish a thought.
I used to watch the last boats from the cottage before taking this job.
I know which boats are home by the rhythm of their oars. Sometimes I stay out just to hear the last one.

reel.name: Reed
questions: Where can I try fishing?
What made you open the shop?
reel.local: Start at the town pond. Oldwater will still be there when you know your rod.
personal: I wanted somewhere dry to mend a line.
I used to carry all my tackle to the Coast in one tin. Everything tangled together.
The drawer marked “spares” is for people who make that same mistake.

exchange.name: Maren
questions: What comes out of Deepwell?
Which stones do you keep?
exchange.local: Ore, gems, and a surprising number of scratched-up carts.
personal: The ones with an odd shape nobody wants to pay for.
My first gem was too dull to sell. I put it on the counter anyway.
I still have it. It catches the morning light for about one minute.

mine.name: Orrin
questions: What should miners know?
How did you start here?
mine.local: Pay attention to the sound of the track. It tells you when a cart is coming home.
personal: Sweeping grit off the rails.
My first shift underground felt longer than a whole winter.
I take the first shift with new miners. It’s easier to ask questions when someone else is carrying the lamp.

market.name: Sable
questions: What’s the market known for?
What do you look for in a stall?
market.local: Things made by people who still live close enough to mend them.
personal: Something someone took the time to finish properly.
I tried selling three kinds of wares at once. I forgot the price of all three.
I like helping new traders set up. Everyone deserves one day where the stall looks better than they expected.

atelier.name: Iris
questions: What makes a good outfit?
Where do you get your ideas?
atelier.local: A small detail you’ll still like after the novelty wears off.
personal: From the colours people bring back from their trips.
I once matched a thread to sunset over Oldwater. By noon it looked completely different.
Now I leave the swatches by the window for a whole day. A colour should feel right in the morning, too.

challenge.name: Beren
questions: How should I start a trial?
Do you still run the trials?
challenge.local: Pick a style you enjoy and learn what one clear feels like.
personal: I do, when the board needs checking.
I missed a timing mark in my own lodge because I was watching the scenery.
I leave my name off the practice list. I like having a place where I can be bad at something.

gather.name: Sorrel
questions: Where do the crews forage?
What do you like to gather?
gather.local: Willow Brook and the meadows are good places to learn what grows here.
personal: The things that smell good even before I know their names.
One crew brought back mud in a neatly labelled sack. They’d left the herbs on the bank.
I kept the label. It’s now on the drawer for things we forgot.

apothecary.name: Willow
questions: What are your brews for?
How do you test a recipe?
apothecary.local: A specific kind of trouble. Read the label before you pack one.
personal: Slowly, and with a notebook I can wash.
A batch from the marsh once turned the stirring spoon green for a month.
I still use that spoon when a new apprentice is afraid of making their first mistake.

tower.name: Vale
questions: What happens in the Spire?
Why do you study echoes?
tower.local: We observe echoes. A practice echo is easiest to learn from when you take your time.
personal: They’re good at showing me what I overlooked.
I spent a week studying the flash before I noticed the pause that came before it.
Now I teach people to watch for the pause. It helps outside the Spire, too.

gate_0.name: Garran
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
gate_0.local: I count everyone heading out. I’m happier counting them back in.
personal: I can walk the gate road in the dark. I still take a lantern.
I used to keep score by how far I could march.
Now a good shift is one where every face on my list comes home.

gate_1.name: Marl
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
gate_1.local: If the lookout flag goes flat, the wind’s about to change.
personal: I always look at the sky before I check my watch.
I learned the flag calls before I learned the streets.
I still write the calls on my glove. My hands remember them better than I do.

gate_2.name: Nessa
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
gate_2.local: People hurry past the pond. I’m paid to notice what they miss.
personal: If the ducks move out of the way, someone is coming.
I know which ducks arrive first.
I used to dislike the quiet shift. Now I trade for it.

gate_3.name: Rooke
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
gate_3.local: Mind the lamp by the west pillar. The stone gets slick when it rains.
personal: I keep a dry rag folded beside my lantern.
I didn’t like the cave until I learned where the wind comes from.
I leave the lamp a little brighter when a new party goes in.

gate_4.name: Dain
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
gate_4.local: If someone says they’ll be right back, I wait until I can see them.
personal: A late party can have my dinner if it means they get back safely.
My first watch felt like standing still for a year.
Now I’ve learned that waiting can be the useful part.

gate_5.name: Sedge
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
gate_5.local: The bridge gets quieter just before the birds settle.
personal: I like the part of the road where you can still see the roofs.
I used to think I needed a sword to be useful on this road.
Most days I just tell lost people which side of the river they’re on.

gate_6.name: Olla
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
gate_6.local: If you see the lanterns coming on, the evening shift is already walking.
personal: These boots are on their third set of soles.
I know the streets by the sound of my boots.
When someone mended the cobbles outside the pavilion, I missed the old rattle for a week.

partner_5.name: Tarn
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
partner_5.local: I take the rear on patrol. Somebody has to spot what we walked past.
personal: I’m better at following tracks than keeping up with conversation.
I used to try to walk as fast as Sedge.
Now I keep my own pace. We spot different things that way.

partner_6.name: Iona
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
partner_6.local: I carry spare wick on the south road. It always gets used.
personal: I check a lantern with my gloves on. That’s how I’ll use it.
My first lantern went out during a rainstorm.
I still carry the wet wick from that night in a dry little pouch.

arena_0.name: Bex
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
arena_0.local: If you’re nervous before a match, watch one round before signing up.
personal: I remember every fighter who looked relieved to lose their first round.
I used to think the crowd only watched the winner.
I hear them cheer for someone who gets up every time.

arena_1.name: Ronan
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
arena_1.local: I check the gate hinges before every match. They’re louder than the crowd.
personal: Anything with a hinge gets a drop of oil on my shift.
I learned to fix hinges because I couldn’t stand waiting for help.
The loudest squeak is gone. I almost miss knowing who’s coming.

harbour_0.name: Mae
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
harbour_0.local: Leave the river mouth clear for the boats coming back in.
personal: I know which board to skip so I don’t wake the boatkeepers.
I learned the harbour by walking it in fog.
I can tell which pier I’m on by how the boards creak.

harbour_1.name: Tobin
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
harbour_1.local: If you’re bound for the Coast, check the wind before you untie.
personal: Give me a loose rope and I’ll find something to do.
I’m better at knots than I am at telling stories.
My best knot is the one I can untie with cold hands.

barracks_0.name: Walt
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
barracks_0.local: A clear call matters more than a loud one in the muster court.
personal: I keep the first instruction short enough to shout in one breath.
I practised commands into a blanket as a recruit.
Now I ask the quietest person in the line to give the first call.

barracks_1.name: Cerys
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
barracks_1.local: If your boots are slipping, your aim is already off.
personal: I count my breaths between shots. Three usually does it.
I used to aim at the middle of the shield every time.
An old coach taught me to look for the opening, then wait until it was real.

barracks_2.name: Holt
questions: What should I know about your post?
What brought you to the Ramguard?
barracks_2.local: I check the straps after drills. Nobody thanks a buckle until it breaks.
personal: When I hear a squeak during a drill, I look at the straps first.
I kept a spare strap for one person on my first watch.
I carry two now. One for whoever asks, one for whoever won’t.

north_west.name: Edda
questions: How’s the gate?
What do you do off duty?
north_west.local: The west hinge sings in cold weather. If it goes quiet, I check it.
personal: I bake when I’m off duty.
I make little buns shaped like the gate stones.
I leave the first tray for the dawn watch. I remember how hungry that shift gets.

north_east.name: Cal
questions: What do you watch for?
Do you like the gate shift?
north_east.local: I watch the road beyond the banners. People give themselves away by how they walk home.
personal: I like being first to see visitors.
My first visit to Crossroads began at this very gate.
I try to greet nervous visitors the way Edda greeted me. A wave is easier than a speech.

carpenter.name: Merrit
questions: What are you working on?
Where did you learn to build?
carpenter.local: A replacement tread for the pavilion. The loose one has been keeping time with the musicians.
personal: My first workbench was a plank across two crates.
The cedar I use for repairs comes through the Coast. I save every sound offcut.
I left one scratch in the pavilion table. It’s where someone learned their first game.

farmer.name: Hale
questions: What’s growing?
Why farm by the river?
farmer.local: Beans by the fence. I plant them high enough that the river has to ask permission.
personal: The ground does half the work if I listen.
Oldwater taught me to read the waterline before I plant.
When the beds flooded, Rowan brought seedlings. The first basket every year goes to the Seedhouse.

market_load.name: Perrin
questions: What’s in the crates?
Do you like the early shift?
market_load.local: Fish from the lake and jars from the Coast. The jars complain louder when I set them down.
personal: An empty cart is a good sight.
My first load was three crates taller than I was. Mira helped me carry the last one.
I still take a corner of the load when someone says they can do it all themselves.

market_sort.name: Edric
questions: Where do the shipments go?
Do you remember every crate?
market_sort.local: South-bank baskets go under cover first. Give me a minute and I can tell you where anything is.
personal: Only the interesting ones, and the ones that leaked.
Someone sent a pebble from Folded Coast marked ‘fragile.’ I delivered it in both hands.
It was a birthday gift from a child who’d never been to sea. I still wrap pebbles carefully.

market_cart.name: Joss
questions: Does the cart always rattle?
What’s your favourite delivery?
market_cart.local: Only if the route needs attention. Right now the cart has a lot of opinions.
personal: Food that’s still warm when I get there.
I once took the wrong turn and brought bread to the lookout.
The guard split it with me. I keep an extra loaf on the cart when I can.

post_sort.name: Nim
questions: How do you sort the mail?
What’s your favourite parcel?
post_sort.local: Town goes on the left. Anything headed up to Oldwater waits for the boat.
personal: I like parcels with drawings on the wrapper.
Someone drew a fish on a parcel that held a boat key. It went straight to the right dock.
I keep a pencil by the window. Pictures help when a parcel has to go farther than you know how to spell.

post_dispatch.name: Pella
questions: Where does the next shipment go?
Have you delivered a parcel yourself?
post_dispatch.local: Downriver. We’re waiting for the boatkeeper to say the wind is right.
personal: I used to do the marina rounds.
A coast delivery sent me home with a jar of salt and an invitation to supper.
I bring the boatkeeper a sandwich on long dispatch days. Somebody did that for me on my first route.

post_rounds.name: Tuck
questions: What are you checking?
What do you like about the rounds?
post_rounds.local: The cart wheels. I’d rather find a loose one here than on the bridge.
personal: I like the streets before the shops open.
I used to race the lamps coming on. Nowadays I stop when the work is done.
I know a bench with a view of the pond. It’s where I go when I finish early.
